item.title: Identifying aligned tensor decompositions across heterogeneous neural datasets
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Kralik, M., Tinelli, S., Kozloski, J., Ponte Costa, R., Sharott, A., Peach, R. L.
Large-scale neural recordings increasingly span many sessions, brain regions and animals, but differences in neuronal sampling make it difficult to identify and interpret shared patterns. We introduce Neuralign, a tensor- based model that jointly aligns and decomposes recordings into components, each pairing a shared temporal pattern with its expression in individual trials and neurons, without requiring matched neurons, matched trials or behavioural labels. In simulations, pooling recordings improved recovery of shared components; in recurrent networks, Neuralign distinguished related from distinct task solutions. In the macaque motor cortex, label-free components recovered the ring-like organisation of reach directions. Across 93 brain-wide mouse recordings, Neuralign discovered a single component that isolated the response to inhibition of the anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM). A reference learned from correct, uninhibited trials revealed inhibition-related activity outside the choice direction on error trials, most strongly in the ALM and thalamus. Neuralign provides an interpretable framework for studying the shared structure of large neural datasets, linking shared patterns to individual trials and recorded populations.

item.title: Direction of oscillatory networks in the human medial temporal lobe reverses across verbal working memory phases
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Choi, D., Han, H.-B.
Working memory (WM) requires neural circuits to change how they interact as information is encoded, maintained and used. Directional oscillatory interactions in the medial temporal lobe (MTL) contribute to memory processing, but how these interactions are spatially organized during verbal WM remains unclear. Here, we analyzed intracranial electroencephalogram and neuronal spiking recorded from the human MTL during a verbal Sternberg task. Theta- and gamma-band activities in MTL showed predominant directionality in the posterior-to-anterior axis during WM encoding, but this direction was reversed to anterior-to-posterior during retrieval. Theta activities reflecting the WM load were more prevalent in left than right MTL, and theta in left MTL coordinated spike timings more strongly. Moreover, interhemispheric interactions showed a predominant left-to-right influence, with posterior-to-anterior interactions enhanced during encoding and anterior-to-posterior interactions enhanced during retrieval. Together, these findings suggest that verbal WM engages a spatially organized MTL network in which the predominant direction of oscillatory interactions changes across task phases.

item.title: State-dependent structure-function coupling reflects dynamic engagement of the brain's structural scaffold
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Pedersen, R., Sala-Llonch, R., Persson, J., Salami, A.
Functional brain organization is shaped by the brain's anatomical scaffold, yet how structure-function coupling varies across cognitive states remains unclear. Across 723 adults from two independent cohorts, we examined coupling using diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging. In the primary cohort, coupling was strongest during movie-watching, intermediate during rest, and weakest during working memory, declining further with increasing working-memory load. The movie-rest difference replicated in an independent sample, challenging the primacy of rest for revealing anatomical constraints. State effects were superimposed on a stable unimodal-to-transmodal cortical hierarchy, with movie-watching preferentially enhancing coupling in sensory and language systems. Regions with more stable functional connectivity across states showed stronger coupling. Older age was associated with lower auditory and somatomotor coupling in both cohorts, alongside heterogeneous increases in association cortex. Together, we show that cognitive context shapes structure-function alignment, supporting a framework of complementary structure-constrained and distributed-integrative modes of communication.

item.title: A Variational Principle for the Emergence of Neural Geometry Underlying Bayesian-Like Behavior
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Serrano-Fernandez, L., Parga, N.
Neural population geometry constrains how task variables are represented and read out into behavior. We propose a variational principle in which learning balances task accuracy and representational smoothness under stimulus-dependent weighting. This balance links stimulus statistics to the shape of a latent neural coordinate. For magnitude estimation, the principle predicts distortions near the edges of bounded ensembles, global affine contraction for Gaussian ensembles, and warping toward high-probability regions for bimodal ensembles. We test the bounded-uniform case in recurrent neural networks trained to reproduce time intervals. Their learned geometries occupy three regimes as the boundary distortions change from too narrow to resolve, to measurable, to extending across the stimulus range. A shape parameter selected from an empirical neural coordinate predicts the nonlinear component of mean behavior through an affine readout, with only behavioral gain and offset fitted afterward. In this bounded-uniform setting, the variational coordinate and Bayesian least-squares mean response have closely matching shapes after affine normalization. These results suggest a variational account of how stimulus statistics shape neural geometry and yield Bayesian-like behavior.

item.title: Non-invasive temporal interference stimulation targeting the hippocampus enhances fast motor memory consolidation
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Pan, X., Taylor, J., Violante, I. R., Grossman, N., Inman, C., King, B. R., Albouy, G.
Converging neuroimaging evidence indicates that the hippocampus is involved in motor sequence learning (MSL) and its consolidation at multiple timescales. However, direct evidence for a causal role of the hippocampus in these processes in healthy humans remains scarce, partly due to the inability of conventional non-invasive brain stimulation techniques to reach this deep brain structure. Here, we used temporal interference stimulation (TIS) - a technique enabling non-invasive stimulation targeted toward deep brain regions - to probe the functional role of the hippocampus in MSL and its consolidation. In two separate experiments, sixty-four young healthy adults (36 females) received, in within-subject counterbalanced designs, active (5 Hz envelope) or control (0 Hz envelope) hippocampal-targeted TIS either during active practice of an MSL task (task-TIS experiment, n = 32) or during the short rest periods interleaved with task practice known to support rapid forms of consolidation (rest-TIS experiment, n = 32). Consolidation was assessed at both the micro timescale (i.e., over the short "micro-offline" rest intervals interspersed with task practice) and macro timescale (i.e., over a 24-hour "macro-offline" retention interval). Our results indicate that TIS targeting the hippocampus during inter-practice rest periods - but not during task practice - significantly enhanced micro-offline gains in performance as compared to control stimulation. While this effect did not carry over to the 24-hour retention interval at the group level, participants with greater stimulation-induced micro-offline gains showed larger overnight performance improvements. These findings provide the first direct evidence that experimental interventions targeting the hippocampus modulate offline motor memory consolidation processes.

item.title: Does a texture-defined frame enlarge the Medusa effect for faces? A preregistered online study with Gabor texture boundaries
item.description:
Relevance: 21% | Source: SocArXiv
Yuki Yamada
The Medusa effect is the tendency to attribute more mind to a person depicted at a lower level of representation (L1) than to a person depicted at a higher level (L2) (Will et al., 2021; Han et al., 2024, 2026). In this online study, Japanese participants view images of two faces on a wall filled with oriented Gabor elements and rate each person on experience, agency, and realness on a 0-10 scale. In the boundary condition, the elements inside a rectangular window around the face on one side (L2) are rotated by 90 degrees, so that a rectangle is perceived from the texture difference alone, without a luminance edge. In the no-boundary condition, all elements have the same orientation. We predict that the Medusa effect (L1 rating minus L2 rating) is larger in the boundary condition than in the no-boundary condition. This study is run in the same session as a separately preregistered study on Kanizsa illusory frames. The sample size is determined by a sequential Bayes factor design.

item.title: Reactivation-dependent amnesia for contextual fear memories in rodents: Assessment of publication bias
item.description:
Relevance: 19% | Source: SocArXiv
Laura Luyten et al.
Research on memory reconsolidation has been booming in the last two decades, with numerous high-impact publications reporting promising amnestic interventions in rodents and humans. However, our own recently- published failed replication attempts of reactivation-dependent amnesia for fear memories in rats suggest that such amnestic effects are not always readily found and that they depend on subtle and possibly uncontrollable parameters. The discrepancy between our observations and published studies in rodents suggests that the literature in this field might be biased. The aim of the current study was to gauge the presence of publication bias in a well-delineated part of the reconsolidation literature. To this end, we performed a systematic review of the literature on reactivation-dependent amnesia for contextual fear memories in rodents, followed by a statistical assessment of publication bias in this sample. In addition, relevant researchers were contacted for unpublished results, which were included in the current analyses. The obtained results support the presence of publication bias, suggesting that the literature provides an overly optimistic overall estimate of the size and reproducibility of amnestic effects. Reactivation-dependent amnesia for contextual fear memories in rodents is thus less robust than what is projected by the literature. The moderate success of clinical studies may be in line with this conclusion, rather than reflecting translational issues. For the field to evolve, replication and non- biased publication of obtained results are essential. A set of tools that can create opportunities to increase transparency, reproducibility and credibility of research findings is provided.
